newsitem.title: USA: Counsel defends disclosure on questioned muni deal.
newsitem.headline: Counsel defends disclosure on questioned muni deal.

text.p: Lawyers for a Cooper Hospital, N.J., bond deal, commenting after reports of an FBI probe, said they told investors everything they were entitled to know about fraud allegations at the Camden facility.
Cooper Hospital officials this week confirmed that the U.S. Attorney's office is looking into the $69 million bond deal, and said they were cooperating with FBI investigators.

At issue is whether the official statement on the deal, underwritten in February by Lehman Brothers, provided potential bond buyers with enough information about losses the hospital suffered over the past few years as a result of fraud.

Part of the controversy arose because the hospital declined to release an audit detailing the losses. Hospital officials said they are pursuing lawsuits, and releasing the report would compromise their case.

Instead, bond counsel on the deal, McCarter & English, said they aggressively questioned hospital officials about the audit and included details about the audit's conclusions in the official statement.
"The disclosure was done properly," Scott Kobler, an attorney at McCarter & English, said in an interview.
In the official statement, investors were told of the 1994 guilty pleas of key hospital officials, and of fraud estimated at the time to have cost Cooper Health System $3.8 million.
The official statement notes that the extent of the fraud was later found to be higher.

"Board and Health System Managment review of more than $1 billion of expenditures over the seven-year period involved identified approximately $21.8 million in expenditures made or controlled by and/or to the individuals involved, which amounts include the aforementioned $3.8 million," the statement says.
The disclosure also says that all of the amounts had been expensed by the system as already incurred, and that measures had been put in place to prevent a recurrence.
"Health System Management believes that the losses did not materially affect past, and will not materially affect future, financial positions or results of operations," it says.
SEC, which oversees federal disclosure regulations on municipal bond deals, has so far not contacted anyone involved in the case, according to officials with the hospital and bond teams.
Kobler of McCarter & English said he does not expect SEC interest, because "there's nothing there."

"It's an open book, other than the audit, which is something that (Cooper Hospital) has claimed under privilege," Kobler said. "We knew about the audit, and we knew in many respects what was in the audit and we asked very tough conclusory questions relating to the audit."
Kobler said he is confident, "based upon the representations of Cooper and their attorney," that everything from the audit that legally needed to be disclosed was disclosed.
Lehman officials declined to comment on the matter.
The FBI has requested copies of the official statement and the audit and was given both, according to officials involved with the deal.
